data.content_ref: inline:The target's core premise is false: it asserts that 'any action-guiding preference necessarily assumes that past success is a reliable guide to future success, which is the definition of induction.' But preferring the better-tested theory for action does not logically require the inductive premise that the future will resemble the past. One can prefer theory B over theory A purely on the grounds that A has been falsified while B has not yet been—an eliminative, deductive choice, not an inductive one. Popper's 'critical preference' is precisely designed to avoid induction: you act on the theory that best withstands criticism, not because you predict it will continue to succeed, but because it is the only unrefused option available and you must choose. The target conflates 'I prefer B because it is the least-worst available option' with 'I prefer B because I expect it to succeed,' smuggling in an assumption about the decision-maker's epistemic state that Popper explicitly rejects. The counterexample shows a decision-maker who prefers B solely because A is logically eliminated, with zero expectation that B will succeed—a rational, action-guiding preference that is entirely non-inductive.
